title: Kunti's word at the door
hookLine: two brothers come home with a princess, and their mother answers without looking
carry: satya: even a careless word is kept true

cards: Someone in the crowd has worked it out. While the kings fight, Krishna watches the brahmin with the bow and the giant with the tree, and turns to his brother Balarama. That one with the tree, he says, is Bhima.
The archer is Arjuna. They didn't die in the fire. Meanwhile, at the potter's house where the family is staying, Kunti waits.
It's late, and her sons haven't come back.

teach.b: Bhima and Arjuna come to the door with Draupadi. They're living as brahmins, on alms, so they call in: look, we've brought alms.
And Kunti, inside, without looking up, answers the way a mother might: share it, all of you. Then she sees who's standing there. A princess, not a bowl of rice.
What have I said, Kunti cries, the text says. Why doesn't she just say oops?

Because in the Mahabharata, satya, truthfulness, sits near the heart of dharma, and a spoken word is something you keep. Kunti didn't mean it, and still she won't let her word go false. But she doesn't force it, either.
She takes Draupadi by the hand, goes to Yudhishthira, and asks how her word can stay true without wrong being done to the princess.
Truth, held with care. Yudhishthira offers Draupadi to Arjuna, who won her; Arjuna says the eldest should marry first.
Then Yudhishthira, remembering words Vyasa once spoke and fearing his brothers could be divided, says she'll be the wife of all.
The Bhagavad Gita, later in this same epic, names the discipline of speech: words that are true, kind and helpful, that cause no one distress.
Hindu grandmothers teach it more simply: don't say what you don't mean, because words count. And then Krishna arrives at the potter's door, and bows at Yudhishthira's feet.

how: Bhiksha, food given as alms, is part of Hindu religious life: renunciants, and in some traditions students, receive food from householders, which is why the brothers, dressed as brahmins, call what they bring home alms.

o: the alms the brothers beg for as wandering brahmins
the choosing Arjuna won, brought home to Kunti's door
a mother's rule that her sons must share all they own

p: answers: share it, all of you
says the eldest should marry first
knows them, and comes to the door

s: Kunti saw Draupadi before she answered
she answered without looking, then saw who it was.
Kunti shrugged off what she'd said
she cried out, the text says, and asked Yudhishthira how to keep her word true.
Krishna recognized the brothers at the swayamvara
he told Balarama the one with the tree was Bhima, and the archer Arjuna.

games.q: you're Kunti. you've just told your sons to share what they brought, and it's a princess. what do you do?
o: laugh it off; it was a slip.
ask Yudhishthira how to keep your word true and do her no wrong.
games.why: she takes Draupadi by the hand and asks Yudhishthira how her word can stay true without wronging the princess. satya, kept with care.

practice: Bring back something you said this week without really looking: a quick yes, a promise called from the other room. Ask Kunti's question about it: how can this word stay true without anyone being wronged?
If you pray, ask for help keeping it; if you don't, just picture one small step that would keep it. Breathe out, and let it rest where you can find it later.

wordCard.voice: Draupadi's swayamvara, brought home. Today: alms announced at the door, a mother's word given without looking, and kept.

orig.note: Sanskrit bhikṣā: alms, food given to those who live by asking; what the brothers announce at the door.

carryVoice: Your line: satya: even a careless word is kept true. Kunti kept hers, with care. Day seven hundred forty-four, done.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Swayamvara Parva (Krishna recognizes the Pandavas; the return to the potter's house; Kunti's words; Yudhishthira's decision; Krishna and Balarama visit)
Bhagavad Gita 17.15 (the austerity of speech: words that cause no distress, truthful, pleasant and beneficial)
